meta.theme: the paradox of tolerance handled by comparing tolerance understood as a temper, which has a quantity and no terms, with tolerance understood as a settlement, which has parties and terms, and settling for the second while denying it the comfort it appears to offer, since the obligation becomes conditional and what is owed is a standing offer answered by conduct rather than by opinion

meta.reviewer_notes: Two conceptions set side by side, one preferred, and then the preferred one denied the comfort it seemed to promise. The final paragraph does three things in quick succession, prefers, concedes and limits, and the tone and inference questions are both decided there rather than in the comparison that occupies most of the passage.
meta.tone: analytical, unsparing about its own conclusion

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the neutral reading, since the first four paragraphs lay the two conceptions out with evident fairness; the fifth opens by calling the second account better, which is a verdict, and then refuses to make it a comfortable one, so neutrality cannot survive the sentence that chooses. Q2's rival is the option that the paradox disappears once tolerance is properly defined, which is half of the passage: the difficulty loses most of its force under the second conception and the last paragraph then reopens two cases and makes the obligation conditional. Q3's rival is the capacity reading, which the second paragraph invites by saying the virtue is measured by how much it will bear; the word names the disposition itself, which the same sentence glosses as a settled cast of mind a person has or lacks. Q4's rival is the option that a group which rejects the terms has placed itself beyond the society's concern, which contradicts the requirement that the offer be kept open and kept real at a yearly cost.

paragraphs.text: The difficulty is easy to state and hard to leave alone. A society that tolerates those who would abolish tolerance is said to be arranging its own end; a society that refuses to tolerate them has abolished it already, by its own hand, and saved its enemies the trouble. The usual way out is a threshold. Tolerate them, the advice runs, until they become dangerous, and then stop. That is sensible, and it does not touch the difficulty, because a threshold is a decision about how much, and the objection is about what kind of thing tolerance is. Two answers to that question are in circulation, and they behave very differently under pressure.

The first makes tolerance a temper: something a person has or lacks, a settled cast of mind towards what he dislikes. On this account the tolerant man is the one who does not mind, or who minds and carries on regardless. The virtue is measured by how much it will bear, and that is exactly why the paradox bites so hard here. A temper has no terms. It has only a quantity, and any point at which it stops is a point at which somebody has run out of the virtue rather than a point at which he has exercised it well. A disposition to endure cannot tell anybody when to stop, because nothing inside it contains that information.

The second makes tolerance a settlement. Two parties who have discovered that neither can defeat the other agree to stop trying, and the agreement has terms: certain questions are removed from the list of things that may be decided by force. Nobody is required to stop minding. People are required to stop acting on what they mind, and to accept the same restraint from the other side. Here the paradox loses most of its force, because a settlement has parties, and a party who will not accept the terms has not been thrown out by an act of intolerance. He has declined an offer.

There is something to be said for the second as a description, quite apart from its convenience. Tolerant societies do not in fact contain much not-minding. Their members dislike one another's opinions as heartily as anybody ever did, and the arrangement survives regardless, which is not what a theory of temper would predict. The institutions that carry the arrangement look wrong for a virtue and right for an agreement: courts, rules about what may be done to a losing side, procedures a person can appeal to against the majority that dislikes him. Nobody builds an appeal procedure to protect a disposition.

The second account is the better one and it is the less comforting, which is the part usually left out. It makes the obligation conditional, and a conditional obligation is the last thing anybody wants to hear about at the moment it is being tested. It leaves two cases unresolved as well: the party who was never offered the terms, and the party who cannot accept them for reasons that are not refusals. What a tolerant society owes the intolerant, on this account, is therefore neither silence nor suppression. It is the offer, kept open and kept real, which is uncomfortable, because keeping it open to people who despise it costs something every year. And the account has a limit worth stating precisely. An offer is answered by conduct. A society may act on a refusal made in action, and may not treat an opinion by itself as the refusal, since the belief was never the thing being asked about.

questions.target_mistake: mistaking four paragraphs of even-handed exposition for the absence of a verdict, when the last paragraph delivers one and then prices it
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: he picks the second account, and in the same breath says it gives less than the reader was hoping for.
questions.stem: The author's tone in the passage is best described as

options.A: analytical, and candid that the account he prefers offers less comfort than it seemed to
options.B: apprehensive about a danger he believes tolerant societies have been very slow to see
options.C: impatient with a puzzle he takes to be an invention of philosophers with time to spare
options.D: neutral between the two conceptions, since each explains something that the other cannot do

explanation.expert_notice: The judgement words are concentrated in one place. The fifth paragraph opens by calling the second account the better one and the less comforting in the same sentence, then lists what it fails to settle, then calls the obligation it produces uncomfortable and costly. Nothing earlier in the passage evaluates anything.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option keeps the verdict and the candour together, which is what that paragraph does. The author decides between the two conceptions on grounds of description, then refuses to let the winner be consoling, saying the obligation is conditional and that two cases remain open. An option that removes the verdict or removes the discomfort has to account for a paragraph built out of both.
explanation.question_type_note: Tone is read from judgement words, not from subject matter. In a passage of comparison the judgement usually arrives late, so the last paragraph carries more tonal weight than the three before it.
explanation.reading_habit: Look for the sentence where an author grades his own conclusion. Writers who say a view is better and less comforting in one breath are telling you their tone in six words.

distractors.why_wrong: Arranging its own end belongs to the first horn of the paradox as the passage reports it, not to the author. He treats the difficulty as a question about what tolerance is, and nothing in his own sentences forecasts a danger or urges anybody to see one.
distractors.seductive_element: The opening sentences are genuinely dramatic, and a reader who takes the statement of a paradox as the author speaking will carry that alarm through the rest.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage takes the puzzle seriously enough to build its whole structure on it, calling it hard to leave alone and showing why the usual threshold answer fails to reach it. Impatience would make the second paragraph, which explains why the paradox bites, unnecessary.
distractors.seductive_element: The remark that the threshold does not touch the difficulty is brisk, and briskness towards one proposed solution reads as contempt for the problem.

distractors.why_wrong: The author chooses. He says the second account is the better one, gives descriptive reasons for it in the fourth paragraph, and then works out what follows from it rather than from its rival.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because four of the five paragraphs really are even-handed exposition, and fairness is habitually mistaken for having no position.

questions.target_mistake: stopping at the third paragraph, where the paradox weakens, and treating the dissolution of the puzzle as the purpose of the passage
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to name the verb and the object: swap one picture of tolerance for another, then say what the new picture leaves unsettled.
questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is

options.A: to warn that a society which tolerates its enemies will not in the end outlive them
options.B: to describe the institutions by which modern societies manage to keep disagreement peaceful
options.C: to replace one picture of tolerance with another, and then to say what the replacement does not settle
options.D: to show that the paradox disappears altogether once the word tolerance has been properly defined

explanation.expert_notice: The structure announces the purpose. Two answers are named at the end of the first paragraph, each gets a paragraph, the fourth argues for one of them, and the fifth spends its whole length on what the winner fails to deliver. The last paragraph is longer than either of the expositions it follows.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option covers both halves of that shape. The replacement is the settlement, argued for as a description because tolerant societies contain little not-minding and build appeal procedures rather than dispositions; the unsettled remainder is the conditional obligation, the party never offered the terms and the party who cannot accept them. A purpose that ends at the replacement leaves the longest paragraph in the passage unexplained.
explanation.question_type_note: Primary purpose is a verb with an object, and both have to survive the closing paragraph. Where an author spends his last and longest paragraph on limits, the limits are part of the purpose.
explanation.reading_habit: Count the paragraphs a candidate purpose accounts for. If the passage's final movement is left over, the candidate has named a stage of the argument rather than its point.

distractors.why_wrong: This is one half of the paradox as the passage states it in order to examine it. The author never endorses either horn, and his answer is that a threshold and a forecast both miss the question of what kind of thing tolerance is.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the most quotable sentence in the passage and it comes first, so a reader who fixes the purpose early takes a stated difficulty for a stated warning.

distractors.why_wrong: The courts and the appeal procedures occupy half of the fourth paragraph and are used as evidence that tolerance looks like an agreement. They are an argument for a conception, not the subject the passage is about.
distractors.seductive_element: They are the passage's only concrete material, and concrete material is what readers remember when they are asked what a passage was about.

distractors.why_wrong: The first clause is nearly the third paragraph's claim, where the paradox loses most of its force, and the word altogether is what the passage refuses. Two cases are left unresolved and the obligation is called conditional, so the difficulty is reduced rather than dissolved.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the passage really does define its way out of most of the problem, and a reader who stops before the fifth paragraph has seen nothing to contradict the word altogether.

questions.target_mistake: taking the commonest modern sense of the word, or replacing the disposition with the measure the paragraph applies to it
questions.prediction_target: The learner should paraphrase from the same sentence, which glosses the word as something a person has or lacks.
questions.stem: As it is used in the second paragraph, the word temper most nearly means

options.A: a settled cast of mind that a person may have or lack
options.B: a readiness to be angered by opposition from other people
options.C: an unusual capacity for putting up with what one dislikes
options.D: the prevailing mood of a whole society at a given moment

explanation.expert_notice: The author defines the word in the clause that introduces it: a temper is something a person has or lacks, a settled cast of mind towards what he dislikes. Everything after that applies a measure to the thing defined, and the measure is not the definition.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is the gloss the sentence supplies. The paragraph then contrasts this kind of thing with a settlement, which has terms, and the whole contrast depends on a temper being a disposition, the sort of thing that comes only in quantities. That is why the paragraph can say a temper has no terms but only a quantity.
explanation.question_type_note: A word-in-context question is settled by the sentence that introduces the word, especially where an author is fixing a term for his own use. The dictionary's commonest sense is placed among the options on purpose.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author writes a colon after a word, read what follows as his definition and use it. He has taken the decision out of your hands, and the options that ignore it are the distractors.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the word's commonest modern sense and the paragraph does not support it. A temper here is what the tolerant man has, not what he loses, and the sentence describes a person who minds and carries on regardless.
distractors.seductive_element: Losing one's temper is the phrase everybody knows, and the surrounding talk of what a person will bear keeps anger in the reader's mind.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph measures the virtue by how much it will bear, which is a statement about how this kind of thing is assessed, not about what the word names. Adding unusual also makes a definition out of a degree the passage never sets.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the sentence about how much it will bear is the paragraph's most memorable, and capacity is what the whole argument about running out depends on.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph locates the thing in a person, twice, saying it is something a person has or lacks and describing the tolerant man who does not mind. The society appears in the paragraph after, as a party to an agreement rather than as the bearer of a mood.
distractors.seductive_element: The phrase the temper of the times is familiar, and the passage's subject really is societies, which makes the larger unit feel like the natural one.

questions.target_mistake: reading the settlement account as licensing action against people whose opinions reject the terms, when the passage makes conduct the only answer to an offer
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the inference will turn on the last two sentences, which say an offer is answered by conduct and not by opinion.
questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred about how a society on the second account should treat an intolerant group?

options.A: It must permit any conduct at all, so long as the opinion behind the conduct is sincerely held
options.B: A group that rejects the terms has by that rejection put itself beyond the society's concern
options.C: The difficulty was never a real one once the two conceptions of tolerance had been separated
options.D: It may act on a refusal that has been carried out, and not on one that has only been professed

explanation.expert_notice: The passage ends by naming a limit and explaining it. An offer is answered by conduct; a society may act on a refusal made in action; it may not treat an opinion by itself as the refusal, because the belief was never the thing being asked about. The third paragraph has already supplied the reason, since people are required to stop acting on what they mind rather than to stop minding.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that limit in the form of a rule. The settlement asks for restraint in action, so the only thing capable of breaching it is action, and an opinion, however hostile, leaves the terms intact. The option also keeps the permission the passage grants, since a refusal carried out is a breach the society may answer.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question rewards the option that keeps both halves of a limit. Where an author says what may be done and what may not, an option giving only one half has dropped the qualification.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage says what an arrangement asks of people, use that to work out what could possibly break it. The answer usually settles every question about how the arrangement may be enforced.

distractors.why_wrong: The settlement restrains conduct and leaves opinion alone, which is the reverse of this. The third paragraph says people are required to stop acting on what they mind, and the last paragraph allows a society to act on a refusal made in action.
distractors.seductive_element: Sincerity is the usual currency of arguments about toleration, and a reader who has absorbed that nobody is asked to stop minding may extend the permission from minding to doing.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage requires the opposite, saying what is owed is the offer, kept open and kept real, and adding that keeping it open to people who despise it costs something every year. Nobody is placed beyond concern by a refusal.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the third paragraph does say that a party who declines has not been thrown out, and that sentence can be read as the society having no further duty.

distractors.why_wrong: The paradox is said to lose most of its force under the second conception, not all of it, and the final paragraph reopens it for two cases and makes the obligation conditional. This also answers a question about the puzzle rather than about how a group should be treated.
distractors.seductive_element: It restates the passage's most satisfying moment, and an option that resolves a difficulty is attractive to a reader who has been holding one for five paragraphs.

vocabulary.meaning_here: a point on a scale at which a rule changes

vocabulary.passage_use: The first makes tolerance a temper
vocabulary.meaning_here: a settled disposition of mind, what a person is like

vocabulary.meaning_here: an agreement that ends a conflict on stated terms
holding only while something else is also true

mentor.challenge: Two accounts of the same word are laid out and one of them wins. Watch the final paragraph carefully, because the author spends it taking back most of what winning seemed to promise.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: The paradox of tolerance survives the usual threshold answer because it is a question about what kind of thing tolerance is, and it weakens once tolerance is understood as a settlement with parties and terms rather than as a temper with a quantity and none, though the settlement makes the obligation conditional, leaves two cases open, and turns what is owed to the intolerant into a standing offer that only conduct, never opinion, can be said to refuse.
mentor.main_idea: Tolerating the intolerant looks like a trap either way out. Setting a threshold does not help, because the trouble is about what tolerance is. If it is a temper, a disposition measured by how much it will bear, the trap holds, since a disposition contains no instruction about where to stop. If it is a settlement with terms, the trap mostly opens, because a party who refuses terms has declined an offer rather than been expelled. The second fits what tolerant societies actually look like. It is also colder: the duty becomes conditional, and what is owed is an offer kept open, which only action can refuse.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Here is the old problem. If a society puts up with people who want to abolish tolerance, it is helping to end itself. If it refuses to put up with them, it has already ended tolerance by its own hand. Neither branch looks good.

The usual escape is to draw a line: tolerate them until they get dangerous, then stop. That sounds fine, but it answers a question about how much, and the problem is really about what sort of thing tolerance is in the first place.

There are two answers about, and they behave very differently.

The first says tolerance is a temper, a kind of person you are. The tolerant person does not mind, or minds and gets on with it anyway. You measure this by how much it can take. And that is exactly why the trap holds under this description, because a temper has no terms, only an amount. Wherever you stop, you have simply run out of it. Nothing inside a disposition to put up with things tells you when to stop putting up with things.

The second says tolerance is a settlement. Two sides work out that neither can beat the other, so they agree to stop trying, and the agreement has conditions: certain questions will not be decided by force. Nobody has to stop disliking anybody. People have to stop acting on the dislike, and to get the same in return. Under this description the trap mostly opens, because an agreement has parties, and someone who will not accept the terms has not been expelled. He has turned down an offer.

The author thinks the second is also the better description of real life. Tolerant societies are not full of people who do not mind; their members dislike each other's views as much as anyone ever did, and things hold together anyway. And look at what carries it: courts, protections for whoever lost the vote, procedures you can appeal to against a majority that dislikes you. Nobody builds an appeals procedure to look after a personality trait.

Then the uncomfortable part. This account is colder than it first sounds. It makes the duty conditional, and a conditional duty is the last thing you want when the duty is being tested. It leaves two hard cases: people who were never offered the terms at all, and people who cannot take them for reasons that are not really a refusal. So what a tolerant society owes the intolerant is not silence and not suppression. It is the offer, kept genuinely open, which is expensive to do year after year for people who despise it. And there is one precise limit. An offer is answered by what you do. A society can act against a refusal that has been carried out. It cannot treat the opinion on its own as the refusal, because the belief was never what was being asked about.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage looks for four paragraphs like a balanced survey and then decides, so readers who fix the tone early record no position at all. The second difficulty is that the third paragraph resolves the paradox and the fifth partially reopens it, which means the satisfying moment and the honest moment are far apart and readers keep only the first. The last paragraph is also doing three different things in nine sentences, preferring an account, conceding what it costs, and stating a limit on enforcement, and the limit is the part most often lost because it arrives last and is stated in the flattest language in the passage.
mentor.author_intention: To move the argument off the question of how much a society should put up with and on to the question of what sort of thing it is doing when it puts up with anything, and then to stop the reader taking the more workable answer as the more reassuring one.

paragraph_journey.note: Tolerate them and you end yourself; refuse and you have ended it already. Drawing a line does not help, because the real question is what tolerance is.
Tolerance as a temper, a kind of person. Measured by how much it bears, so wherever it stops it has simply run out. No terms, only an amount.
Tolerance as a settlement with terms. Nobody has to stop minding, only to stop acting. Whoever refuses the terms has declined an offer, not been expelled.
Real tolerant societies are full of people who do mind. Courts and appeal procedures look like the furniture of an agreement, not of a disposition.
Better, and colder: the duty becomes conditional, two cases stay open, what is owed is a standing offer, and only conduct can refuse it.

mentor.tone_progression: It opens with the crispness of a well-worn puzzle, stays flat and expository while each conception is set out, becomes quietly argumentative at the appeal procedures, and turns exacting at the close, where the author names his preference and immediately lists what it fails to give him.
key_transitions: 'That is sensible, and it does not touch the difficulty' (paragraph 1): the usual answer is set aside and the question is changed from how much to what kind.
'Here the paradox loses most of its force' (paragraph 3): the second conception does its work, and the words most of its force are the whole of the qualification.
'The second account is the better one and it is the less comforting' (opening of paragraph 5): the verdict and its price arrive in a single sentence.
mentor.misunderstanding: The common wrong model is that the passage solves the paradox by defining tolerance correctly, which is the third paragraph read as the conclusion. It is not: the resolution is partial by the author's own wording, two cases are reopened, and the duty is made conditional. The second wrong model reads the settlement as permitting a society to move against people whose opinions reject its terms. The last two sentences forbid exactly that, and the third paragraph explains why, since what the settlement asks for is restraint in action and not agreement in belief.
mentor.traps_summary: The set offers a horn of the paradox as the author's warning, the concrete institutions as the subject of the passage, the partial resolution stated as a complete one, the everyday sense of a word the author had just defined, and permission to act against an opinion in place of permission to act against conduct. Sorting each option by which paragraph it belongs to answers all four.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage sets two definitions of one word against each other, the argument is almost never about which definition is nicer; it is about which one makes the problem tractable, and the questions will be built on what the winning definition still fails to do. Read the last paragraph of such a passage for the word most, only, or conditional, because that is where an author marks the difference between a difficulty solved and a difficulty reduced.
mentor.real_world: The same choice between a temper and a settlement runs through arguments about free speech at work, about the rules of a professional body, and about what a platform owes its worst users. In each, it matters whether you are being asked to feel differently or to accept terms, because only the second gives you anything to point at when the other party stops keeping them.
mentor.takeaway: An arrangement asking you to stop acting is answered by what you do; an arrangement asking you to stop minding can only be answered by how much you can bear.
mentor.reflection_question: Where in your own life are you keeping an offer open to somebody who has refused it in words but not yet in conduct?
